Personally, echo chambering is inevitable (and indeed, one should not try to avoid echo chambering, although that is another matter). Anything that builds community innately causes an echo chamber. The question in my mind is not "how do we prevent echo chambering", but "how do we prevent the problems associated with echo chambering".

I have a few ideas along that front. One off-the-wall idea goes along the line of not preventing echo chambering. Effectively, you compute the similarity score for the votes of all users, and then, for each user, weight vote weights by how similar the people who voted for them compared to that user. So you see things that are upvoted by people who vote like you (and downvoted by people who vote unlike you!)

It has a few interesting consequences. For one, it completely mitigates vote brigades . It also mitigates puppet accounts (creating secondary accounts for purposes of upvoting your posts, downvoting other posts, that sort of thing).

It gets especially powerful if you can create multiple voting profiles within an account.

I have yet to figure out a good way to mitigate the inherent O(n^(2)) complexity of that approach, however. Having to compute the voting similarity between every pair of users gets impractical very quickly.

Mod transparency and the site not pushing an agenda. One of the reasons reddit could become an echo chamber so easily is that moderators would often censor views they disagreed with, and the community often wouldn't even realize it because mods weren't very open with their deletion policies. Maybe each subverse could have an associated subverse that automatically tracks posts that mods delete. If it's something illegal or doxxing then they can just delete it, or if the original poster wants it gone, but other than that it gets recorded so users can see what the mods are actually censoring. It would let users know when the mods are pushing one view and silencing another

I'm a distiller.

I would like to say that my day is like in an advertisement. Some castle in Scotland, or a wooden shack in woods, where I spend my day tasting samples from aged barrels and sharing drinks with my friends while playing a fiddle or something.

Truth is, I wake up around three or four, and bike over to a small building, kitty corner from a bowling alley. While the coffee is brewing, I do actually sample the barrels to see where we are in the aging process. It's not elegant glass. I'm pulling off in plastic syringes into a measurement cup to analyze color. I think squirt some in my mouth to get a taste of it before food and coffee ruins my taste buds. I then spend the next hour taking apart the still and cleaning every part. It used to take two hours, but I now have it down pat. I then put everything together and start the stills up. While they heat up, I have a cup of coffee and spend an hour doing janitorial work. Mopping floors, cleaning lab ware, taking inventory. Once the stills are cooking, I consult the spreadsheets to give me a rough sense of when I'm going to make "cuts". I taste what's coming off the stills. Rest fo the day is running tests on the fermentation tanks, preparing more raw materials for fermentation, pitching yeast and whatever else needs to me done....and mopping.

No time for a fiddle or anything. Just hour after hour of work on my feet.

Day isn't over, though. We're a small company. If we need to get our product to the store, we're going to deliver it ourselves. We'll also do events where we sample what we make, and I spend far too much time in bars talking about us, instead of just enjoying time at the bar.

I wouldn't trade it for anything.

No degree or anything required for my job. Not too many distiller jobs out there, so you have to go in knowing your stuff. I spent about ten years, on my own, learning about fermentation and the alcohol business.
